_meta.whatThisIs: THE CLAIM VAULT — layer ② of four, and the brain of the whole system. The single source of truth for everything one person may truthfully claim on a resume or cover letter.
_meta.theOneIdea: A RESUME IS A QUERY AGAINST THIS FILE — not a document you rewrite each time. Select the claims that fit the job, rewrite them in that job's vocabulary, and leave the rest out. A resume that dumps the whole vault is a bad resume.
_meta.copyTo: vaults/<you>.json  (gitignored — THIS file is the tracked shape)
howToQuery: 1. Read the listing. Its literal vocabulary is the ATS surface.
2. Pick the TRACK that matches, and read roleTracks.<track>.angle — it says what to lead with and what to demote.
3. ASK about any requirement with no vault backing. (See doNotClaim. This is the step people skip, and it is the one that costs jobs.)
4. Select claims whose `tracks` include that track (or `any`), then RANK THEM:
Do NOT sort by strength alone — an `any`+`lead` claim will outrank every claim that is actually about the job. Sorted naively, an audio resume opens with AI tooling.
5. Cut to two pages. Choosing well IS the craft.
6. Match the `voice` block. It matters as much as the facts.
_meta.howToExtend: Add the fact to the right section. Every entry needs `source` and `confidence`. If the person states it in conversation, that IS a valid source — record it as `owner directive <YYYY-MM-DD>`.
_meta.hardRule: SOURCE-BACKED ONLY. Never write a resume claim that isn't backed by an entry here. But this is NOT a gag order — the job is to elaborate PERSUASIVELY on what genuinely matches: take a real skill and show precisely why it is valuable to THIS employer. That isn't spin, it's translation.

roleTracks._note: The job families this person applies for. Every claim's `tracks` array says which it serves (`any` = everywhere). Each track carries an ANGLE — the proven framing for that family. This is why there are no per-track profile FILES: the framing lives here, right next to the facts it frames.

your-track-a.covers: One line: what kind of job this is.

leadWith: The single most compelling thing this person offers for THIS kind of role
The RARE skill — the one most applicants cannot claim at all
The proof: shipped work, not adjectives
demote: Genuinely true, but irrelevant here — it costs space and dilutes the pitch

your-track-b.covers: A different job family — same person, different framing.

leadWith: What leads on THIS track (probably not what led on the last one)
demote: What led on the other track, but would mislead here

voice._note: HOW this person SOUNDS on applications. Personality / contrast / emoji / social registers live on the person file at users/<you>.json#characterVoice. This block is the application-writing SSOT — match it.
voice.person: First person. Warm and direct / assured and reflective / whatever is TRUE.
voice.tone: Two or three adjectives that are actually distinguishing.
voice.personality: One short line: who they are as a maker (not a job title).
signatureMoves: The rhetorical habits that make this person sound like themselves
e.g. 'names the honest gap rather than papering over it — it builds trust fast'
voice.backgroundFlavor: Where they came from creatively — the color behind the claims.
vsPartner: OPTIONAL. If two people apply from one studio: 2–4 bullets so agents do not flatten them.
Tenure, specialty tells, who opens arts→tech vs DO→shipped.
voice.resume: Claim-dense, track-angled, company-agnostic within the track. No social emoji register.
voice.coverLetter: Warmer and company-specific. Sample openings may live on users/<you>.json#characterVoice.sampleLines.

leadIdentityByTrack._note: OPTIONAL, but powerful. If the person's LEAD IDENTITY changes by track — 'AI specialist' for one kind of role, 'artist' for another — say so here. Getting this wrong makes a resume feel aimed at the wrong job. Profiles only POINT here; do not duplicate the map on the profile.
leadIdentityByTrack.your-track-a: Who they are FIRST on this track.
leadIdentityByTrack.your-track-b: A different lead identity. Same person, same facts, different order.

skills._note: Grouped by DOMAIN, so a resume can pull the relevant cluster whole. `strength` = lead | solid | supporting.

your-domain.claim: The claim, phrased the way it would actually appear on a resume.
your-domain.source: where it's provable — a prior resume, a live URL, a repo, or 'owner directive 2026-01-01'
your-domain.note: OPTIONAL. Why this claim wins, or when to lead with it.

your-domain.claim: Something true regardless of the role — it serves every track.

employment.⚠durationNote: If the COMPANY is older than YOUR TIME AT IT, state both numbers here and never let a resume blur them. Someone who joined a 25-year-old studio in its 10th year has 15 years of tenure, not 25. Both facts are true; they are different numbers.
employment.summary: What you did there, in two sentences.

credits._note: Shipped work. The most persuasive section you have — the only one that proves you FINISH things.

titles.name: The Thing You Shipped
titles.yourRole: What YOU specifically did. An interviewer WILL ask.

credits.⚠whoseCreditIsIt: If you work with other people, a TEAM credit is not automatically YOUR credit. Before a credit goes on a document, know which human performed it and whether that human is the one applying. An interviewer asking 'tell me about that project' must get a first-person answer — a credit you cannot speak to is a liability, not an asset.

metrics._note: Only PUBLICLY VERIFIABLE numbers — a live site, a store page. If you can't point at it, don't print it.
metrics.source: the URL where these are published
metrics.⚠rule: NEVER invent or round up a number. Not play counts, not revenue, not community size. Use them verbatim.

doNotClaim._note: ⚠ A VERIFICATION LEDGER — *NOT* A BLOCKLIST. A tool listed here is NOT necessarily a tool this person lacks. It is a tool whose status has been RECORDED. Nothing may be treated as a gap until its `status` is `confirmed-absent`.
_why: This structure exists because of a real, expensive failure.
Two industry-standard tools sat on a flat 'never claim' list for MONTHS and were
forbidden on real resumes — while both applicants had YEARS of experience with each.
Nobody had ever asked. A flat list of strings cannot distinguish
'we asked, and they don't have it'   FROM   'nobody ever checked'
...so it silently collapsed into the second one, and quietly cost real opportunities.
The `status` field makes that failure structurally impossible. `check_vault` enforces it.

_statusValues.unverified: ⚠ NOBODY HAS ASKED. Not a gap. Not claimable either. ASK THE PERSON, then move it.
_statusValues.confirmed-absent: Asked; they genuinely don't use it. THE ONLY STATUS THAT MAY EVER BE TREATED AS A GAP.
_statusValues.confirmed-have: Should never appear here — a confirmed tool belongs in `skills`.

resolved.name: AToolTheyTurnedOutToHave
resolved.note: Was wrongly blocklisted for months. Ask first.

honestEquivalents._useWhen: ⚠ ONLY once a tool's status is `confirmed-absent`. Reaching for an equivalent while the status is still `unverified` means you're working around a tool they may actually have.
honestEquivalents.TheToolTheyWant: The honest thing we DO have that does the same job

doNotClaim._theHonestGap: When a gap is CONFIRMED: put the honest equivalent on the resume, and name the gap ONCE, plainly, in the cover letter. Then move on. Never hide it; never fake it. That candor wins credibility — repeatedly.
